title: Medium is launching a new note-taking app called TK
snippet: Think of TK as Google Docs meets group chats, meets blogging. | Image: David Pierce / The Verge For the first time ever, Medium is becoming more than just a blogging platform. The company is launching a new app, called TK, that combines note taking and journaling with something resembling a private social network. The app is meant to get you writing more, and help you share that writing with friends and fans. And it's part of a much bigger idea about blogging, and a much broader thesis about the state of the internet. "I don't think we've actually had a launch of anything important since 2017," Medium CEO Tony Stubblebine tells me over Zoom, a few days ahead of the company's biggest launch in apparently almost a decade. That was when … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
For the first time ever, Medium is becoming more than just a blogging platform. The company is launching a new app, called TK, that combines note taking and journaling with something resembling a private social network. The app is meant to get you writing more, and help you share that writing with friends and fans. And it’s part of a much bigger idea about blogging, and a much broader thesis about the state of the internet.

“I don’t think we’ve actually had a launch of anything important since 2017,” Medium CEO Tony Stubblebine tells me over Zoom, a few days ahead of the company’s biggest launch in apparently almost a decade. That was when Medium’s then-CEO, Ev Williams, decided to quit chasing ad dollars and become a subscription business. “It’s clear that the broken system is ad-driven media on the internet,” Williams wrote at the time. “It simply doesn’t serve people. In fact, it’s not designed to.” Medium began charging for access to most content. “We got out of the attention economy,” Stubblebine says now.

The trend Williams saw back then, though, has only accelerated and metastasized. AI companies are hoovering up any content they can get their hands on, legality be damned; search engines and chatbots are sending less and less traffic back to the web. Medium, like most websites on the internet, relies on Google for a huge portion of its traffic — in the time of Google Zero, that’s an existential risk. “When Google started taking away all the traffic,” Stubblebine says, “what I told them is that this hurts us, but it also hurts you, because I’ll just tell you what my product roadmap is going to do: I’m going to switch to private blogging… We’re just going to take everything underground.”

All of which brings us back to TK, an app and network that has no use or need for Google referrals. The idea behind TK is fairly straightforward: It’s a barebones note-taking app, with emphasis on daily journal-style notes and longer-form writing. The app itself is nice enough, like an ultra-minimalist take on Evernote, but it’s the stuff around the writing that has Stubblebine most excited.

For one thing, you can point an AI model at your writing, and use it to help organize or make sense of all the notes you’ve been taking, by searching through your notes or asking for feedback on your writing. “TK” is both the name of the app and a shortcut in it: type the letters (which writers use frequently as a placeholder — they’re easy to find later, since the letters T and K hardly ever appear next to each other otherwise) and you can summon the model to fill in a bit of information for you. Stubblebine refers to “Unix pipes” a few times in our conversation, and his idea is to use the large language models to do some of the grunt work of both creating and managing notes.

Once you’ve written something – and Stubblebine emphasizes that it doesn’t have to be a blog post — you can then share it however you like. You can share it via links or email the way you’d share a Google Doc, and collaborators can write, comment, and leave emoji reactions. You can also add your writing to what TK calls Libraries. Stubblebine calls the Libraries concept “private blogging,” which is a good metaphor. The early Libraries I’ve seen in the app are mostly centered around a topic, and people can contribute their writing on that topic. There’s no public face to any of it; it’s just a blog for and by its authors. Sometimes a few of them, sometimes a few hundred. There are groups sharing their ongoing book projects, swapping recipes, and posting poetry drafts, all for the eyes of only the other people in the group. It’s blogging meets group chats.

This concept of private blogging is a big part of the future of Medium. “Medium is, at some level, performative,” Stubblebine says. “You have to want to share yourself with the world.” But in a post-Google world, he says, that’s essentially impossible. TK doesn’t measure pageviews or reward authors for getting traffic. “This is a community that’s going to give you feedback and encouragement,” Stubblebine says. “It’s not about the drive to be noticed.” Features like this, he says, are coming to the broader Medium platform soon.

TK is now available, for free, via apps for the web, Android, and iOS. (Stubblebine says a native desktop app is also coming soon.) If TK works, though, it could be a crucial new way for Medium to make money. Obviously, Stubblebine says, there are ways to make money from private and paywalled content. That’s the newsletter business. But also, he wonders, what if there’s a way to package up all the best stuff from the Recipe Box library and charge people, or AI agents, for access? “The generic web is getting dumber and dumber,” Stubblebine says. If AI is the future, “it needs to be based on this layer of human intelligence.” And all that intelligence might be better off outside the confines of the Google algorithm.

excerpt:
For the first time ever, Medium is becoming more than just a blogging platform. The company is launching a new app, called TK, that combines note taking and journaling with something resembling a private social network. The app is meant to get you writing more, and help you share that writing with friends and fans. And it’s part of a much bigger idea about blogging, and a much broader thesis about the state of the internet.

“I don’t think we’ve actually had a launch of anything important since 2017,” Medium CEO Tony Stubblebine tells me over Zoom, a few days ahead of the company’s biggest launch in apparently almost a decade. That was when Medium’s then-CEO, Ev Williams, decided to quit chasing ad dollars and become a subscription business. “It’s clear that the broken system is ad-driven media on the internet,” Williams wrote at the time. “It simply doesn’t serve people. In fact, it’s not designed to.” Medium began charging for access to most content. “We got out of the attention economy,” Stubblebine says now.

title: iOS 27.2 adds three new ways to customize your iPhone
snippet: iOS 27.2 launched last week with a lot of new features, and also several ways you can customize your iPhone. Here’s what’s new for iPhone personalization. more…
fullText:
iOS 27.2 launched last week with a lot of new features, and also several ways you can customize your iPhone. Here’s what’s new for iPhone personalization.

#1: Exclude apps from Siri and Search

Inside Settings ⇾ Siri there’s a new ‘Excluded Apps’ section in iOS 27.2. This makes it easier than ever to remove certain apps from being accessible to Siri, Search, and more. Apple says:

Apps added to the list below will be excluded from Siri, Search, and suggestions.

With Siri AI, Siri can do more than ever before. But if there are certain apps you want off-limits, whether for privacy reasons or otherwise, you can add them to this list. For example, if there’s an app with a similar name to something else, adding it to the ‘Excluded Apps’ list can ensure Siri won’t mistakenly think you’re referencing that app anymore.

#2: Customize Messages suggestions

iOS 27.2 adds a new Messages feature called Suggestions that I’m a big fan of. When relevant content is detected in a conversation, you might see a Suggestion appear underneath a message. For example, if a friend asks you to do them a favor, you might see “Add to Reminders” below the message.

By default there are five supported categories of Suggestions:

Add to Calendar

Add to Reminders

Add to Notes

Show in Maps

Flights and Packages

You can fully customize these to your own preferences and needs. Just go to Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ Messages ⇾ Suggested Actions to disable whichever Suggestions you don’t want to see.

#3: Apple TV user profiles

Historically, Apple TV has only ever supported user profiles on tvOS. It’s an odd limitation considering every other streaming service offers profiles across platforms.

But finally with iOS 27.2, profiles are now available on iPhone too, letting you customize the content in the Apple TV app based on who’s watching.

Choosing a profile not only gives you personalized recommendations from Apple TV, it also lets you keep the ‘Continue Watching’ queue separate for each person. And if you’re setting up a profile for a child, you can set content restrictions too.

title: Nvidia will investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy
snippet: In a memo to the company, Huang admitted that he had an affair.
fullText:
Nvidia’s board of directors announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation.

Nvidia also published a message that Huang sent to the company admitting that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed (though he didn’t mention her by name). A memo circulating among U.S. policymakers earlier this year claimed that Alice Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Huang added that he’d “fallen short” of his responsibility to the company.

“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” he said.

As the AI race between the United States and China heats up, chips, especially Nvidia’s chips, have been a major focus. Huang also seems to have a close relationship with President Donald Trump, who’s been a cheerleader of the AI (or “superintelligence”) industry.

In its announcement, Nvidia’s board said that it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or company secrets were compromised. It also said that Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” and that the board has “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team.”

The investigation will be conducted by independent directors working with outside legal counsel.

In response to earlier reports about the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, Nvidia had said that the pair’s interactions were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with customers.

Other companies involved in the AI boom have warned employees to be wary of possible spies, including those offering sex or romance.

When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

		

Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor. Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. He lives in New York City.

title: ‘Cyclon’ uses an old Google Pixel to let AI do literally everything for you – who wants this?
snippet: As the AI era continues to find its footing in the consumer market, “Cyclon” is a new smartphone/software experience that, to start, is reusing old Google Pixel phones with a software experience that literally uses AI to do every little thing. And my biggest question is just… who actually wants this? more…
fullText:
As the AI era continues to find its footing in the consumer market, “Cyclon” is a new smartphone/software experience that, to start, is reusing old Google Pixel phones with a software experience that literally uses AI to do every little thing. And my biggest question is just…  who actually wants this?

The pitch of Cyclon, the founders explain in a video on Twitter/X, is to “[build] an AI phone to replace the iPhone.” And the central experience seems to be… talking to a chatbot. Examples in the video include telling the AI to “handle my notifications” and letting it monitor a WhatsApp message and reply to a friend asking for photos by grabbing those photos from your gallery without you as the user needing to touch the device. 

Other examples on the company’s website have mixed utility at a glance. “Order my usual on DoorDash” and calling a courier to let them into a building certainly could be useful, but “tell the group chat I’m running ten minutes late” only to have the AI send the message on WhatsApp “in your words” not only seems like a waste of time, but a pointless disconnect from reality (as is all too common with these AI ventures).

The one thing that caught my attention here is building apps on demand and being able to share them. The example given is a language learning app tailored to a specific vacation. It’s a really cool idea, though one I would imagine will have some rocky edges. Google is on a similar track with Gemini Intelligence’s “Create my widget” feature (on that note, when is that releasing on phones Google?), and I’d imagine Gemini will be able to do the same thing in time.

	

The actual hardware side of things is also… interesting.

Cyclon says that it has a working prototype of the idea running on Google Pixel 8a units, and it’ll ship “first-batch” backers one of those units with their $199 pre-order of a later “Cyclon Phone” that itself is expected to cost $699 – so you’re getting two phones for $699. That alone seems a little questionable in the midst of RAMageddon, but I digress. 

That “final” phone hardware… sure is something.

There are some good ideas here, some big promises, but more than anything I just want to know who actually wants to use a phone like this.

I’m all for the idea of AI making my life a little easier (despite finding hardly any ways it can do that so far), but sending everything through a chatbot that does everything in the background and even generates “your words” for responses to my friends and family just sounds awful. And the state of social media isn’t exactly helping matters here. Twitter/X is 90% AI replies for engagement for this sort of thing, and Cyclon is paying influencers to boost that engagement too, so genuine reactions just seem impossible to find. 

Sound off in the comments below if you’re an actual human with an opinion on this one, because I’m dying to know what real people think of this.

Follow Ben: Twitter/X, Threads, Bluesky, and Instagram

title: Google Gemini rolling out ‘Memory summary’ with everything it remembers about you
snippet: Google Gemini now offers a “Memory summary” to “view, edit, and delete what Gemini Apps understands about you.” more…
fullText:
Google Gemini now offers a “Memory summary” to “view, edit, and delete what Gemini Apps understands about you.”

On the web, you can access this new experience from Settings > Personal Intelligence (or gemini.google.com/personalization-settings).

This loads a list with categories like: The Essentials (“snapshot of your core background, location, and key relationships”), Career & Professional Projects, Travel & Daily Gear, Media & Entertainment, and Fitness & Lifestyle. Each has several bullet points with specific details.

The text field at the bottom lets you “Add or remove details.” For example:

	

To add info: “Add to my memory that I speak Japanese.”

To remove info: “Remove my old phone number from your memory.”

Google says “Gemini may ask follow-up questions if your request is ambiguous to ensure your summary remains accurate.”

The pencil icon in the top-right corner lets you make broader edits. In the three-dot overflow menu, you’ll find “Memory history” to see “when specific information was added or modified.”

Officially, this feature is available for Google AI subscribers in US English with Keep Activity and Memory enabled. We’re not seeing this rolled out on Android or iOS yet, but the experience should be similar.

title: Do You Speak Geek? 5 Tech Terms That Endure, and 5 That Got Defragged
snippet: Level up your vocab with these tech phrases that’ll give you major rizz.
fullText:
Real talk: I’m not that up to speed on today’s tech vocabulary. That realization clocked me over the head this week when the Scotland-based Collins dictionary came out with its list of new and notable words for 2026. The words include p(doom), which refers to the probability of AI-caused doom; mogging, meaning to outshine or upstage someone; friendslop, a type of low-budget video game played among friends; and ghost jobs, jobs advertised with no real position or intent to hire someone.

Vibe-coding, which was Collins’ Word of the Year for 2025, refers to a conversational way to teach an AI model without typing in all that pesky code. Enshittification, which the American Dialect Society chose as its 2023 Word of the Year, means the gradual, profit-driven decline in the quality of, well, I guess, everything.

Maybe you know and use these terms regularly; maybe you don’t. But, in an effort to stop myself from becoming that Steve Buscemi faking-it-in-high-school meme, I wanted to lay out some tech terms that have a permanent home in the popular lexicon and the words, phrases and abbreviations that haven’t quite stood the test of time. (Note to self: Stop saying “emoticon.”)

			

More from CNET

Five tech terms that survived

Selfie: You know what a selfie is; my mother, on the other hand, may not. The word for taking a photo of yourself with any camera-enabled device was first coined in 2002 on an Australian internet chat forum, of all places, but didn’t become mainstream until 2013.

Content creator: “Influencer” also works here, to refer to a person who shares information on a tech platform and builds an audience of online followers. A related word, “parasocial,” refers to the one-sided relationship listeners or viewers may have with the creator or influencer, who, in contrast, doesn’t know they exist.

Podcast: The Oxford Dictionary named podcast the Word of the Year back in 2005. Since then, the term, which is a mashup of iPod and broadcast and refers to a digital program made available on-demand for streaming or download, has remained relevant. The iPod, however? Not so much. It was discontinued in 2022.

WFH (work from home): The trend of working from your own home via computer saw a substantial uptick during and after the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic. According to a 2022 survey by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, 23% of Americans work remotely.

Unfriend: The New Oxford American Dictionary‘s 2009 Word of the Year became popularized thanks to Facebook, but the term that means ending a friendship has actually been around for quite some time. NPR called it “the Sleeping Beauty of words,” as the term dates back to the 17th century, when it basically meant the same thing.

The ones that got away

Metaverse: Remember when Mark Zuckerberg poured like $80 billion into a virtual reality project that was being touted as the internet platform of the future? The metaverse and its flagship app, Horizon Worlds, were announced in 2021. Five years later, it all fell apart. Now, Zuck is investing a ton in AI, which he’s touting as the internet technology of the future. Second verse, same as the first?

NFT: Just a couple of years ago, you couldn’t go online without reading about NFTs. Nonfungible tokens are digital identifiers to certify ownership of, well, a digital thing of value. Heck, remember when President Donald Trump released an NFT? After the boom in popularity, and the subsequent crash in value of most of them, the term NFT has all but left the public consciousness.

World Wide Web: It’s the internet, folks. Or, the information superhighway if you’re nasty.

Defrag: Back in my day, when we needed better performance from our Windows-based computers, we’d defragment the hard drive. There were plenty of tools you could use to do so. Apparently, this is no longer a thing people do, which is fun, since I still like to use the term in everyday situations. While we’re at it, I’ll be right back. I need to go defrag the car.

Emoticon: Technically, emoticons are made from standard keyboard characters read sideways, such as 🙂 to generate a smiley face. Emoji are graphical images that you can select in various communication programs. (Sometimes, if you try to type an old-school emoticon, the program you’re working in will just grab it and turn it into an emoji.) These days, we just say emoji, even if the word sounds more like a dessert.
excerpt:
Real talk: I’m not that up to speed on today’s tech vocabulary. That realization clocked me over the head this week when the Scotland-based Collins dictionary came out with its list of new and notable words for 2026. The words include p(doom), which refers to the probability of AI-caused doom; mogging, meaning to outshine or upstage someone; friendslop, a type of low-budget video game played among friends; and ghost jobs, jobs advertised with no real position or intent to hire someone.

Vibe-coding, which was Collins’ Word of the Year for 2025, refers to a conversational way to teach an AI model without typing in all that pesky code. Enshittification, which the American Dialect Society chose as its 2023 Word of the Year, means the gradual, profit-driven decline in the quality of, well, I guess, everything.

title: Automattic debuts a platform to deploy vibe-coding apps amid a changing internet
snippet: Automattic aims to compete with the likes of Lovable with Spacefast.
fullText:
WordPress has been a crucial technology and content management system for websites like TechCrunch. Now, WordPress.com owner Automattic is responding to the changing state of the web by debuting a new service called Spacefast, which will allow users to deploy vibe-coded websites and apps.

Spacefast is designed to provide infrastructure for the vibe-coded apps, including databases, authentication, file uploads, emails, and analytics, to make them functional websites, apps, or services. The product competes with the likes of Lovable and Emergent, which offer both interface and rails for vibe-coded apps, but in a more open way.

Users can connect Spacefast with other agents and chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, Hermes, OpenClaw, Grok Bot, Muse, Pi, Cursor, OpenCode, and Amp. Alternatively, they can connect a Git repository to Spacefast to get started.

The product is headed by Batuhan İçöz, who worked on it during one of the company’s hackathon sprints earlier in the year. At that time, he worked on the company’s cross-platform messaging app Beeper and said that he often got Vercel links from his non-technical friends while exploring vibe coding.

“I thought there had to be a better way for everyone to set up and deploy their projects. Automattic already has good infrastructure, but we have been traditionally associated with just WordPress. I thought, why do I have to use Cloudflare when we have a CDN (content delivery network) just as good? So I started working on what was called Stattic and now Spacefast,” he told TechCrunch over a call.

An Office-themed game on SpacefastImage Credits:Spacefast

İçöz eventually disseminated the solution to his friends and added more features to make the product more dynamic. Automattic soft-launched the product in September to get feedback before today’s launch. The company has seen varied use cases of their product, with people and organizations using it for internal mockups, slideshows, and offer-related websites. However, that’s not the only competition Spacefast has. Productivity and design software like Figma, Canva, and Notion have launched products that sit at the intersection of vibe coding, mockups, and presentations.

İçöz thinks that, compared to something like Lovable, Spacefast has the advantage of giving users a choice of their agent and using the solution their way. The counter-argument might be that a certain kind of user wouldn’t want to choose and just have everything figured out for them.

Spacefast said that it also has the advantage of being within Automattic to launch solutions like web analytics, WordPress integration, and e-commerce features (through WooCommerce) easily to compete better with the whole lot. 

“For enterprises, the problem right now is IT sprawl, as their marketing teams are churning out landing pages on services like Lovable, and they want to consolidate and work with a company that understands the enterprise needs. With our existing products, we have experience serving enterprise customers,” İçöz noted.

A Saturday morning TV-styled YouTube experince on SpacefastImage Credits:Spacefast

A challenge for newly minted products in the AI world is to retain people post-launch. Users might get excited to try out a new product, and then move on to the new shiny thing within days or weeks. İçöz is cognizant of the fact and said that he expects people to churn, as they might not be interested in making apps at all.

“I think what we need to do as a product is make sure that when you build something with SpaceFast, it is so easy, and the results are so much better than without Spacefast,” İçöz emphasized.

Many websites and publishers are struggling with dwindling traffic due to AI chatbots and summaries, right now, to the point that Google itself saw its ad revenue growth drop. İçöz acknowledged that people are making websites with ChatGPT or Claude now as compared to deploying something on WordPress, and he said some sites won’t need a content management system at all as the web expands.

Spacefast comes amid turbulent months at Automattic. In an OpenAI/Sam Altman-style saga, the company’s board forced CEO Matt Mullenweg out, but he was back in control within days. The rebel board was eventually replaced, and the interim CFO left within weeks of appointment. In October, TechCrunch reported that the company had begun layoffs across several properties and more cuts were expected.

title: Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution
snippet: At 10 cents per million input tokens, Ember is significantly cheaper than frontier competitors like Haiku and Luna.
fullText:
Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet. In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”

Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.

Image Credits:Meta Superintelligence Labs

At 10 cents per million input tokens, Ember is significantly cheaper than frontier competitors like Haiku and Luna. Not only that, it’s cost-competitive with open-source competitors like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash. 

Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness. In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”

With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio. The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model.”

Ember is the fourth model released under Meta’s Muse brand, following the mid-weight Spark (released in April), Spark’s open-source twin Glimmer (released in August), and the Wonder frontier model (released in October). The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success, with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.

title: Samsung’s next cheap phone will have a much bigger battery than the Galaxy S26 Ultra
snippet: According to a new report, Samsung’s upcoming mid-range smartphone is getting a big battery upgrade that outdoes that company’s current $1,400 flagship. more…
fullText:
According to a new report, Samsung’s upcoming mid-range smartphone is getting a big battery upgrade that outdoes that company’s current $1,400 flagship.

GalaxyClub reports that the Samsung Galaxy A38 will ship with a 6,000 mAh battery. That’s a 20% jump over Samsung’s typical 5,000 mAh batteries that have been in Galaxy A series phones for the past few years, and is also a 20% jump from the company’s current flagship Galaxy S26 Ultra.

Compared to the likes of many other Android phones on the international market, 6,000 mAh isn’t huge. Honor, for example, launched new phones with 10,000 mAh batteries just a couple of weeks ago. But in the context of Samsung, this is a welcome step forward. The company finally embraced silicon-carbon in its latest foldables and, while it’s unclear if that’s what we’re seeing here, it’s very obvious that Samsung is making a push to increase its battery capacity moving forward.

Based on the Galaxy A37’s launch date, the Galaxy A38 is likely to make its debut in early 2027.

	

Galaxy S27 is rumored to make some minor battery upgrades as well.

title: Motorola Signature 27 gets Pixel’s Gemini Intelligence features with Rambler, Create My Widget
snippet: Motorola is adopting Google’s Gemini Intelligence features in the first major expansion beyond Pixel, with Gboard’s Rambler and more supported. more…
fullText:
Motorola is adopting Google’s Gemini Intelligence features in the first major expansion beyond Pixel, with Gboard’s Rambler and more supported.

Motorola Signature 27 goes official with true flagship specs and a $1,599 price tag

While Google’s Gemini Intelligence is technically supporting Samusng’s latest Galaxy devices too, it’s Motorola that’s opening the floodgates beyond the Pixel lineup. The new Motorola Signature 27 is officially getting support for the bulk of Google’s new features, including “Create My Widget” which, so far, has only been available on Googlebook.

Supported Gemini Intelligence features on Motorola Signature 27 include:

Create My Widget

Gboard Rambler

Gboard Sign-to-Text

Gemini task automation

Taking those one by one, “Create My Widget” is, again, the most intriguing addition. Google announced this feature early this year but, even for Google Pixel phones, it’s not yet gone live. That’s presumably soon to change, seeing as Motorola’s launch date for this device is November 19 and the company confirmed that this will be available out of the box on that date.

	

Regardless, the feature itself allows users to describe the functionality they want in a widget to Gemini before the AI spits out a functional widget.

	

Gboard Rambler and Sign-to-Text are also supported here. The former supports taking long-winded voice-to-text prompts and cleaning up filler words and even add formatting, while Sign-to-Text translates American Sign Language via video to English text.

Finally, Gemini task automation allows users to assign certain tasks to Gemini, with the AI then running the bulk of the task through supported apps such as Uber and DoorDash in the background. This is also available on Pixel and select Samsung Galaxy devices.

Motorola Signature 27 pre-orders are open now, with the flagship priced at $1,599 in the US.

title: Report: Apple and Samsung outperform rivals as smartphone chip shipments tumble 21%
snippet: According to Counterpoint Research, Apple and Samsung were the only major smartphone chip vendors to gain market share in Q3 2026, as global shipments declined 21% year-over-year. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
According to Counterpoint Research, Apple and Samsung were the only major smartphone chip vendors to gain market share in Q3 2026, as global shipments declined 21% year-over-year. Here are the details.

At this point, most 9to5Mac readers are probably familiar with the challenges that smartphone vendors have been facing due to rising memory costs, and how Apple has managed to weather the impact better than many of its competitors.

Over the past few months, many reports have noted that while most smartphone vendors raised prices more than once throughout the year, Apple held off on increasing iPhone prices until September, with the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series.

Those same reports have been showing the iPhone outperforming the broader market in smartphone, even as the industry experiences a sharp downturn.

That said, Counterpoint Research recently published a report (via MacMagazine) examining how rising memory costs and slowing smartphone demand have affected the global smartphone chip market.

According to the report, Apple remained in third place among smartphone chip vendors in the third quarter, with its market share increasing from 17% in Q3 2025 to 21%.

MediaTek still led the global smartphone SoC market with a 28% share (down 6 percentage points year-over-year), followed by Qualcomm with 22% (down from 25%).

After Apple, UNISOC ranked fourth with 13% (down from 14%), while Samsung remained in fifth with an 8% share, up from 6% in Q3 2025. Other manufacturers went from a 4% share to 8%.

Overall, the market saw a 21% decline year-over-year, though the report didn’t disclose how many chips were shipped during the quarter.

Commenting on the numbers, Counterpoint Research Senior Analyst Shivani Parashar said:

“We saw three notable flagship chipset launches in September 2026, based on TSMC’s 2nm process node: Apple’s A20 series, MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 series. These launches are expected to boost premium smartphone SoC shipments in Q4 2026, although volumes are still likely to remain below Q4 2025 levels.”

Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects global smartphone chip shipments to decline 20% year-over-year in 2026, followed by another 3% to 4% drop in 2027. The research firm also expects memory prices to continue rising next year.

During its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings call, Apple described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” warning that further increases would continue to put pressure on its profit margins in the coming quarters.

title: Google’s AI search fumbles leave schools in the lurch
snippet: Good morning, and happy Ocarina of Time day to all who celebrate. Oh, and speaking of celebrating: congratulations to the real winners of the midterms, YouTube and Twitch streamers. Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe. more…
fullText:
Good morning, and happy Ocarina of Time day to all who celebrate. Oh, and speaking of celebrating: congratulations to the real winners of the midterms, YouTube and Twitch streamers.

Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

It’s hard to overstate how reliant US school districts are on Google. Almost every school board in the country purchases Chromebooks for their students, many of whom are able to take them home and treat them as personal laptops. IT and procurement managers like them because they’re relatively cheap and offer zero-touch enrollment, which lowers upfront and ongoing maintenance costs. Teachers also like them because Google Classroom is relatively intuitive and ChromeOS is optimized for most other web-based education platforms.

	

But this reliance on Google’s tech stack comes at a cost: school boards are forced to comply with the company’s capricious terms of service, in particular when it comes to the creeping proliferation of AI across its products. 

Things came to a head earlier this week when the New York Times reported that changes to the Google Search experience in schools will require opting into Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and, perhaps most importantly, AI Overviews. The move actually comes after Google was pressured to make student AI usage opt-in. Google’s justification: search and AI are now “deeply integrated” in the tech stack, so disabling one means disabling the other.

Google’s alternative to AI Overviews is a new Guided Learning feature, which replaces search’s primary function — solving a problem — with a step-by-step guide that helps a student understand said problem.

Former FTC Chair Lina Khan took to X to decry the move: “Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI,” she said. “This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service. Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened. As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”

I have a feeling Google will need to walk back this decision in some form. As 9to5’s Ben Schoon points out, it’s comically easy to disable AI Overviews in the current version of Google Search, and it doesn’t seem to have a detrimental impact on the subsequent results. But Google is likely worried that if it is forced to carve out versions of the search experience for specific user bases, revenue from its burgeoning AI Overviews ad business may be impacted.

Even if Google sticks to its proverbial guns, the move exposes a rift between the public, particularly parents, and the tech giants pushing AI on their users. Furthermore, the AI boom has had a direct impact on educators’ ability to purchase new hardware and upgrade old Chromebook fleets, since component prices have increased by as much as 5x over the past year. Some lower-income districts are even recalling Chromebooks from students, reverting to a shared laptop pool to save money.

✉️ Inbox

Redmagic 12 Pro review: You’ve never gamed on a phone like this before. We talked about this phone on The Sideload this week: as Android gets better for games, I think gaming phones will be increasingly important for Android.

The Sideload 050: The phones Samsung and Google won’t make

Google has fixed Android Auto issues on Samsung Galaxy phones running One UI 9 [U]

Google confirms Android’s new ‘Family Hub’ feature, and this is what it looks like. Android is getting a bit more family-friendly.

Xiaomi confirms Android 17 HyperOS 4 rollout schedule for these devices

Galaxy Z Fold 8 sales spike amid iPhone Duo release and ‘crackgate’ debacle. The iPhone Duo’s display issues may not yet constitute a scandal, but Samsung’s category lead has never seemed so assured.

Google confirms something was draining Pixel Watch batteries, fix rolling out. Pixel owners seemingly can’t catch a break.

Android Auto 18.1 update rolling out with additional prep for light mode and redesign. Another minor redesign is coming to what is arguably the best version of Android out there.

Google’s Stadia Controller dream lives on in the $50 Xbox Nano Controller. I need this little guy.

‘Cyclon’ uses an old Google Pixel to let AI do literally everything for you – who wants this? Nobody, Ben. Nobody.

ChatGPT has hit roughly 20% of Google Search volume, OpenAI says. This is a staggering number achieved in only four years. It’s no wonder Google is freaking out.

Peak Design’s new wireless charging stand pulls double duty, literally. I saw prototypes for these way back at CES in January, and the final versions look way more polished. Looking forward to trying them.

Google Messages redesigning pinned chats and moving search

Google Photos now lets you turn off background music in Memories. Thank goodness. I genuinely hate this feature.

Google will fix Nest devices that didn’t adjust for Daylight Savings, breaking alarms and more. Oh, Canada.

Microsoft says it now sucks less to use a Windows PC with 8GB of RAM. Seems like Google isn’t the only company doubling down on efficiency.

Three months in, Galaxy Z Fold 8’s cameras aren’t enough, and Fold 9 might not fix it. Ben’s absolutely right about this: I love my Fold 8, but its cameras are straight-up terrible.

The first Snapdragon phone with Android Linux Terminal support is here

Nothing teases screen-less product launching next month, ‘couldn’t have been an app’. This certainly sounds like something that records your every interaction. Couldn’t Bee, right?

‘Enough Phone’ is an Android phone roughly the size of iPhone 13 Mini, launching in 2027. I have to respect the gumption of releasing a phone that will almost certainly be a one-off, but is this what people are really after in 2027?

Henry Cavill builds 16-bit ‘Mustache Protocol’ game on Googlebook for a good cause. This is not doing the Googlebook brand any favors.

➡️ FWD:

For a much less complicated relationship with Google Search, try its Ocarina of Time Easter egg. Search for “Zelda” or “Ocarina of Time,” then tap the Master Sword to travel back to a 1998-style results page, complete with Link’s sound effects. It’s a trip down memory lane to a time when, as even Google acknowledges, things were a whole lot simpler.

Was AI on the ballot? According to Ben Thompson at Stratechery, it was in a big way. Democrats and Republicans both rejected data centers, but Democrats want to actually pass some regulation reining in the hyperscalers’ and frontier labs’ ambitions.

First we were short on compute, but that ramped; now we are short on memory, but that will ramp; we were coming close to being short on power, but that will be rectified. The final constraint is political, and that may be the most imposing constraint of all. Not only is it harder to solve, but it actually interferes with solving the other constraints. Many of the theories about AI assume that it becomes a commodity; I think it’s just as likely we are looking at scarcity for much longer than we expected, which will have ripple effects on everything.

Is it possible to pass broad AI regulation that will slow down an industry that has been allowed to run unchecked since Trump’s reelection in 2024? And is it in the best interest of these companies to support it, even if it means a short-term slowdown at a time when the two biggest AI labs, Anthropic and OpenAI, are about to IPO?

Some fascinating developments in the $6.3 billion Binance hack: turns out it was yet another case of social engineering. A Binance engineer was lured into a fake job interview, before which he downloaded malware that let hackers breach his computer and, eventually, others on the network.

🗑️ Trash

After my discussion with Will last week about the death of browsers, it came as no surprise to learn that Brave is being sued by the New York Times for copyright infringement. Brave is accused of scraping paywalled material from sites like nytimes.com and selling access to it through a search API to AI companies, which use it as training data. Yes, it’s difficult to earn money as a browser maker (see Arc for another compelling example), but this is particularly egregious, even for a company familiar with shady business practices.

Like what you just read? Subscribe to Inbox today and get it in your email every Tuesday and Thursday morning. Got feedback? Send us an email.

You can also support us by becoming a 9to5Google Pro member, starting at just $5/month. You get bonus podcast episodes, access to our members-only Discord server, and lots more.

Thanks for reading, and have a great day. I’ll talk to you on Tuesday.

—Daniel

title: Meta’s Horizon+ looks to become Meta VR+ and include 3D movies
snippet: Meta Horizon+ is rumored to be changing its name to Meta VR+ and may start including movies in addition to games with the subscription price. more…
fullText:
Meta Horizon+ is rumored to be changing its name to Meta VR+ and may start including movies in addition to games with the subscription price.

Meta’s quest (ahem) to distance itself from the Horizon era is in full swing, and the latest rumor says it’s time for the company’s Game Pass-like subscription to change its brand name. VR leaker Nori posted a screenshot on X showing a handful of 3D movies coming to the Meta VR Plus service. Considering there is no such Meta VR Plus service currently, the obvious conclusion is that Meta Horizon+ is being renamed once again.

Meta Horizon+ currently includes over 100 games with its $7.99 per month subscription and is similar to Microsoft’s Xbox Game Pass service in many ways. Unironically, Meta Horizon+ also includes the basic Xbox Game Pass tier with over 50 Xbox games playable via the Game Pass cloud. Meta offers a 3-month trial with every new Meta Quest purchase.

The new Meta VR+ service is purported to include 3D movies as well, although we don’t yet know if this will be included in the regular $7.99 per month rate, or if Meta will be introducing additional content tiers, as services like Netflix, Disney+, Xbox Game Pass, and others do. Based on the screenshot, these will be big-name movies and are likely positioned to enhance the value of the upcoming $1,300 Meta VR Glasses, although all the same content will work on existing Meta Quest 3 units.

	

Meta has been slowly distancing itself from the “Horizon” name ever since the beginning of this year, when its VR division got a big reset. In a February blog post, Samantha Ryan, the VP of Content at Meta’s Reality Labs, spoke about the changes to the company’s strategy, including the loss of most in-house VR gaming studios. Since then, several prominent VR developers from Meta have gone on to create independent studios, including the super-popular Supernatural exercise app.

Meta then decoupled the unpopular Horizon Metaverse from its headsets, moving it to mobile-only, and has been removing the “Horizon” name from just about everything since then. Meta Horizon+ looks to be the latest big change, as the company moves toward “Meta VR” branding, which is clearer and separates its VR division from mobile and smart glasses efforts.

title: iPhone Air 2 is coming next year, here’s why it has more to prove than ever
snippet: Next spring, Apple will take the stage to unveil the second-generation iPhone Air to the world, after taking a bit more time to go back to the drawing board and incorporate a second camera into the design. That said, iPhone Air is no longer the flashy cool phone, now iPhone Duo is. fullText:
Next spring, Apple will take the stage to unveil the second-generation iPhone Air to the world, after taking a bit more time to go back to the drawing board and incorporate a second camera into the design. That said, iPhone Air is no longer the flashy cool phone, now iPhone Duo is.

With that being the case, it seems obvious to me that iPhone Air 2 will need to appeal to a wider audience, beyond just the enthusiast crowd.

iPhone Air wasn’t an incredible seller. That said, it was still an incredible marvel of engineering – proving that you can still pack a largely flagship smartphone experience in such a thin design. It wasn’t perfect though, and the compromises alongside its higher price tag meant it only appealed to a small audience. 

Now that iPhone Air 2 won’t have the shiny-new-thing factor going for it, it seems almost imperative for Apple to address some of the key shortcomings of the original iPhone Air.

We already know Apple is going to address two of the biggest ones: adding a second camera, as well as a larger battery capacity.

iPhone Air concerns don’t end there, though. There’s also compromised speakers, a compromised connectivity and charging experience, and a compromised camera experience.

iPhone Air has a single mono earpiece speaker. Audio on it isn’t excellent. Luckily, with iPad mini 8, Apple introduced acoustic display – which allows speakers to play through the display glass. Perhaps some of that tech can be taken for iPhone Air 2 to improve the subpar speaker experience.

Another major drawback is connectivity and charging. iPhone Air only supports USB 2, while the Pro iPhones support USB 3. Does this matter to most consumers? Maybe not. When the iPhone Air fetches very close to Pro pricing though, it should offer it. On the charging front of things, iPhone Air only supports 20W MagSafe and 25W fast charging, compared to 25W MagSafe and 60W fast charging on iPhone 18 Pro.

	

Lastly, the camera. I expect the camera quality to still be limited as a result of smaller sensors, but there are a few things you miss out on with iPhone Air: RAW support, cinematic mode, and macro mode. The latter is more of a result of the phone lacking an ultrawide camera, so ideally we’ll see macro come to iPhone Air 2.

All in all, iPhone Air 2 needs to have a firm position in the lineup. If it’s going to come within $100 of a Pro iPhone, it should offer an experience close to that. The fact that it’s thin should be just another feature, rather than it being a justification for compromise.

title: macOS 27.3 adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look
snippet: Starting with macOS 27.3, users can preview Markdown files with proper formatting directly in Quick Look. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Starting with macOS 27.3, users can preview Markdown files with proper formatting directly in Quick Look. Here are the details.

Quick Look gets Markdown support on macOS 27.3

Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and new tools for third-party developers.

Among the smaller changes coming to the Mac is a welcome improvement to Quick Look. As of macOS 27.3 beta 1, .md files are rendered with proper formatting directly in Quick Look, rather than displaying their raw Markdown syntax.

Apple has been expanding Markdown support across its platforms, including the ability to import and export Markdown files in Notes. Markdown has also become increasingly important with the rise of AI agents, which use .md files to store instructions, context, and other information.

In fact, as Federico Viticci noted today on X, Apple’s new Siri AI app skills feature also uses Markdown-based SKILL.md files, allowing developers to provide instructions that help Siri perform complex tasks within their apps.

For the uninitiated, Markdown is a simple text formatting syntax created by John Gruber in 2004, and has since become widely used for writing documentation, publishing content online (including this very post), and, more recently, providing instructions to AI agents.

Here’s how Gruber describes Markdown:

Markdown is a text-to-HTML conversion tool for web writers. Markdown allows you to write using an easy-to-read, easy-to-write plain text format, then convert it to structurally valid HTML.

In practice, this means you can create headings, bold text, lists, and links using just a few simple characters. And, starting with macOS 27.3, you’ll be able to preview the results directly in Quick Look, without having to open the file in a separate app.

title: Meet the 20 first-place apps from RevenueCat’s Shipaton 2026
snippet: A cozy habit tracker, a smarter snippet library, and a rooster that wants you out of bed: this year’s Shipaton winners offer plenty of new apps to explore. RevenueCat’s annual app-building competition drew 3,985 project submissions in 2026, according to its winner announcement. Across the 20 first-place categories, developers tackled everyday frustrations, built inventive games, and found new ways to connect people. You can get a look at every first place winner below, and read RevenueCat’s full winner announcement for every more. more…
fullText:
A cozy habit tracker, a smarter snippet library, and a rooster that wants you out of bed: this year’s Shipaton winners offer plenty of new apps to explore.

RevenueCat’s annual app-building competition drew 3,985 project submissions in 2026, according to its winner announcement. Across the 20 first-place categories, developers tackled everyday frustrations, built inventive games, and found new ways to connect people.

You can get a look at every first place winner below, and read RevenueCat’s full winner announcement for every more. 

Mio turns everyday habits into a cozy game

1st place • Grand Prize Winner

Keeping a routine is easier when there’s something to look forward to. Mio pairs self-care and habit tracking with a pixel companion that grows as you make progress. Check off habits, earn coins, and unlock new companions and collectibles, with friends and groups adding a social reason to keep going.

Mio took Shipaton’s Grand Prize, with RevenueCat highlighting its revenue and growth in a crowded habit-tracking market.

App Store  |  Google Play

Boop makes every dog walk a collecting adventure

1st place • #BuildInPublic

That dog you met on your morning walk can become part of your collection. Boop identifies cats and dogs and turns their photos into stickers for a digital book, giving pet lovers a playful reason to pay attention to the animals around them.

Creator Taiwo Omisore’s “100 Boops” challenge took the app into the real world, where printed pet portraits and conversations with owners helped shape the product. That hands-on approach earned Boop first place in #BuildInPublic.

App Store  |  Devpost submission

Nitelore puts neon racing in your pocket

1st place • Best Game Award

If you have fond memories of futuristic arcade racers, Nitelore has a familiar appeal: hovering vehicles, neon tracks, and plenty of speed. Chase your own ghost in time trials, take on combat races, or compete online.

Free tracks offer a starting point, while paid unlocks and daily and weekly challenges give players more to explore. RevenueCat’s Best Game judges singled out the art direction, effects, and haptics.

App Store  |  Google Play

See as Me makes color blindness easier to understand

1st place • RevenueCat Peace Prize

Explaining how you see color can be surprisingly difficult. See as Me: Colorblind makes that conversation visual, using a split-screen camera to compare different types and degrees of color blindness. A shareable link lets someone else see the comparison without installing the app.

Developer Javier Jiménez drew on his own experience with protanopia. That personal perspective helped the app earn the RevenueCat Peace Prize.

App Store

Clucky gives your alarm clock a personality

1st place • RevenueCat Design Award

Clucky’s rooster is determined to get you out of bed. Turning off an alarm can require solving a problem, moving around, or finding an object, bringing a little friction to the temptation to snooze.

Its personality runs through the entire interface, including a time picker that uses the rooster’s scrolling eyes and yellow beak. That consistent character, animation, and attention to detail earned Clucky the RevenueCat Design Award.

App Store

Adversary adds a twist to the memory game

1st place • Catvertising Award

Adversary starts with a familiar challenge: flip cards and find matching pairs. The catch is a hidden Danger card with no matching partner. Reveal it, and an ad becomes part of the board you’re trying to remember.

That idea earned Niv Ben-porath’s game the Catvertising Award. Players can continue with ads after an initial ad-free period, or choose a permanent unlock that removes ads and adds difficulty options.

App Store

Bubble Games brings everyone’s phones together

1st place • Next Gen Award

Put a few phones on the table, and Bubble Games turns their screens into a shared game board. Objects move between devices as friends compete in minigames, including a virtual hot potato.

Built by four software engineering students at Université Laval, the Next Gen Award winner uses the phones people already have to create a shared activity. Its Shipaton submission includes ten minigames. The winner announcement links to the Android release on Google Play.

Google Play

GRIDLOCK gives tic-tac-toe room to grow

1st place • HAMM Award (Help Apps Make Money)

GRIDLOCK takes a game everyone knows and adds up to four players, online rooms, and eleven special moves. The result offers more ways to disrupt an opponent’s plans than the familiar three-by-three board.

Its HAMM Award win recognizes how the business model fits the game: a shared Credits currency connects rewarded ads, optional packs, and a subscription, while core modes remain free. Players can choose the option that fits how often they play.

App Store

Just Add starts dinner with what you want to eat

1st place • Influencer Award – Nutrition & Healthy Eating: Abbey’s Kitchen

Just Add begins with a craving. Type what you feel like eating, describe it aloud, or take a photo, and the app suggests three meals built around it, adding protein, fiber, and healthy fats to round out the plate.

Shopping support, hands-free cooking, and remembered preferences help carry the idea through to dinner. The winner of Abbey’s Kitchen’s nutrition challenge also impressed judges with a dinner-host feature that accounts for other people’s preferences.

App Store

SnipStash keeps reusable content close at hand

1st place • Influencer Award – Productivity: Christopher Lawley

The reply you send every week, the PDF you keep hunting for, and the image you paste repeatedly can all live in SnipStash. It organizes reusable text, images, and files across iPhone, iPad, and Mac, with a keyboard, Mac quick palette, hotkeys, and Shortcuts bringing them within reach.

Private iCloud sync connects the library across devices. Its speed and native interface helped it win Christopher Lawley’s productivity challenge.

App Store

Rehearse helps you practice the difficult conversation

1st place • Influencer Award – Career Coaching: Leadership Heather

Knowing what you want to say and saying it aloud are different things. Rehearse – Hard Conversations gives you an AI counterpart to practice with before a difficult workplace discussion.

Choose from 33 prepared scenarios or bring your own situation, then review feedback on clarity, empathy, assertiveness, and structure. A prep card helps you take the useful points into the real conversation. The app won Leadership Heather’s career-coaching challenge for its focused, straightforward approach.

App Store  |  Google Play

Game Magnet saves the game you spotted in a video

1st place • Influencer Award – Gaming: Mr Lewis Blogs Gaming

You see a game in a short video, mean to look it up later, and forget its name. Game Magnet lets you share the clip to identify the games and save them to your backlog.

Processing happens in the background, with a notification when the result is ready. Shelves, ratings, and ranked lists help organize what comes next. The app won Mr Lewis Blogs Gaming’s challenge by making discovery and keeping track of games easier.

App Store

FeelGood offers movement that fits your day

1st place • Influencer Award – Yoga & Fitness: Simone Sharice

FeelGood: Movement Menu starts with a short check-in about your energy, available time, and how you want to feel. It then offers a small menu of movement, with an appetizer, main, and optional sides.

The options span yoga, Pilates, strength, walking, stretching, and breathing. Rest is part of the experience, too. Yusra Salam and Ameena Malik’s app won Simone Sharice’s yoga and fitness challenge, with judges praising its calm, inviting design.

App Store

BoatBrawl gets friends into the same battle

1st place • Ship Kotlin Everywhere

BoatBrawl brings arcade boat battles to a group of up to eight players. Steer, fire, and scramble through interactive arenas, with bots and shared-screen play offering more ways to join in.

Rehaan Cubes and Ashwin K M used Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform to bring the game across phones and computers, including iOS, Android, Mac, Windows, and the web. Its smooth browser play helped it take JetBrains’ Ship Kotlin Everywhere award.

App Store  |  Google Play

Trazo gives golf videos a broadcast-style finish

1st place • Most Viral App

Trazo: Golf Ball Tracer adds a ball-flight line to your own golf videos. Select the ball twice to start, and the processing runs on the phone.

Julian Praest’s app won Most Viral App for the way its team introduced the product through organic content. Golf humor and practical advice set up the tracer reveal, making the finished video part of the pitch. For golfers, the appeal is simple: make the shot easier to follow when you share it.

App Store

Grandfolio helps collectors identify their next find

1st place • Best App for Galaxy

One Piece Card Game collectors know that similar-looking cards can be very different finds. Grandfolio helps identify artwork variants, manage duplicates, and track collection prices and progress.

The Best App for Galaxy winner impressed judges with layouts that adapt to folded, tabletop, and open-screen use. There’s an App Store release for Apple users, too, making this a relevant discovery even if your collection starts on an iPhone.

App Store  |  Google Play

Let’s Get Support focuses on the people giving support

1st place • Replit’s Idea to Income

Let’s Get Support by 3Dadz is designed for partners, parents, and friends affected by someone else’s addiction. Check-ins, journaling, boundary-setting tools, and local resources give those supporters a place to focus on their own needs.

Joshua Burgess and Aaryn B. built the app from community conversations in British Columbia, using Replit to turn the idea into a live product. It won Replit’s Idea to Income award. The announcement links to its Android release.

Google Play

PoquitoTalk helps everyday conversations cross languages

1st place • The Growth Loop Award

PoquitoTalk: Bocas del Toro turns English into local Spanish voice notes for WhatsApp and helps translate the replies. The recipient doesn’t need to install the app, keeping the conversation in a tool people already use.

Creator Dorien Van den Abbeele drew on years of life in Bocas del Toro. Its Growth Loop Award recognizes extensive growth experiments and an honest account of what the measurements could show. The announcement links to Google Play.

Google Play

Parky! puts useful park updates on your Lock Screen

1st place • Keep Them Coming Back Award

Parky! combines wait times, dining availability, and memories from Disney and Universal visits. Built by former Disney Cast Member Chase Van Derrick, it aims to offer useful help throughout a park day.

Dining alerts can become conversations on the Lock Screen, where you can ask about another time or restaurant. Alongside queue Live Activities and recap messages, those interactive notifications helped Parky! win the Keep Them Coming Back Award.

App Store

In Your Own Words makes room for a minute of practice

1st place • Funnel Vision Award

In Your Own Words offers short, real-world speaking scenarios and feedback on pace, hesitation, and filler words. Speech analysis takes place on the phone, giving users a way to practice the words before they need them.

Natasha Wilson’s app won the Funnel Vision Award for connecting a web quiz, a relevant practice deck, and a web purchase that unlocks access in the app. The introduction to the product begins before the download.

App Store

Winner • Conflict of Interest Award

Friendpire turns the idea of a board-game night with friends into a shared hex-tile world. Gather resources, build farms and docks, and grow an empire together. RevenueCat employee Erik MacInnis built the game to make it easier to stay connected with friends who rarely find time to play.

Friendpire won the separate Conflict of Interest Award, which was open to RevenueCat and sponsor employees and judged by Shipaton participants. It is included here as an optional sidebar and is not part of the 20 first-place count above.

App Store

Discover your next app

From a useful tool for the workday to a game for your next night in, Shipaton’s winners show how much can come from taking an idea all the way to a shipped app. Explore the winners above, or browse RevenueCat’s full announcement for more apps from the competition.

Explore all Shipaton 2026 winners  |  Learn more about Shipaton

title: Apple releases first iOS 27.3 public beta with redesigned Health app and more
snippet: Apple has released the first iOS 27.3 public beta for iPhone. The update brings back the redesigned Health app that briefly appeared during iOS 27.2 testing. It also adds vertical tabs in Safari, gives Siri AI more to do across Apple’s apps, and makes the iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand. more…
fullText:
Apple has released the first iOS 27.3 public beta for iPhone. The update brings back the redesigned Health app that briefly appeared during iOS 27.2 testing. It also adds vertical tabs in Safari, gives Siri AI more to do across Apple’s apps, and makes the iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand.

What’s new in iOS 27.3 public beta 1

Apple released the first iOS 27.3 developer beta on November 3. The biggest change is the redesigned Health app, which didn’t make it into the final iOS 27.2 release.

On iPhones that support Apple Intelligence, the new Insights tab brings together trends from sleep, activity, and more. The Longevity tab includes Health Age, which uses Apple Watch data to show how your health metrics compare with what’s typical for your age.

Here are a few more changes to try:

Safari: Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode let you move your tabs to the side and darken websites that don’t have their own dark theme.

Siri AI: New actions in Apple apps let you ask Siri to make and save a playlist, schedule an iMessage to send later, or create a Journal entry.

iPhone Duo: Reachability shifts content toward either side of the unfolded display so it’s easier to reach with your thumb.

StandBy: More customizable clock faces come to other iPhones, with options for colors and complications.

Apple Fitness+: Gym Strength builds a four-week lifting plan around your goals and the equipment you have.

For more changes, check out our full iOS 27.3 beta 1 roundup.

How to install iOS 27.3 public beta 1

Back up your iPhone, then sign up for the free Apple Beta Software Program with the same Apple Account you use on your iPhone.

Go to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates and select iOS 27 Public Beta. Return to Software Update and tap Update Now when iOS 27.3 appears. If you’re already on the public beta track, you can check for the update directly in Software Update.

Are you installing the iOS 27.3 public beta? Let us know what you’re trying first in the comments.

title: First Android XR ‘Intelligent Eyewear’ glasses go on pre-order next week
snippet: Warby Parker announced today that the first Android XR audio glasses will be available for pre-order on November 12. more…
fullText:
Warby Parker announced today that the first Android XR audio glasses will be available for pre-order on November 12.

Officially, these are being referred to by all the parties involved as “Intelligent Eyewear.” Warby Parker shared the following in its earnings call today: “One week from today, on November 12, we’ll begin accepting pre-orders for our first Intelligent Eyewear collection and look forward to delivering customer orders during the holiday season.”

After pre-orders open next Thursday, the glasses will actually ship “during the holiday season.” It’s unclear whether that means shipping just before Thanksgiving week or going into December.

Running Android XR, the glasses feature underlying hardware manufactured by Samsung and powered by Qualcomm chips. Warby Parker, along with Gentle Monster, is responsible for the design.

	

Warby Parker

These are the audio-only glasses without an in-lens display and paired with a camera. You can control them via voice and the side touchpad.

Throughout the year, we’ve seen two variants from each partner, and there presumably will be more designs.

This pre-order tease before the full announcement somewhat matches how the Googlebook got a date before its full unveil a week later.

title: Apple staff accused of signing up customers to subscriptions without consent; company responds
snippet: Repair technician turned consumer rights advocate Louis Rossmann recently accused Apple store staff of signing up customers to the company’s services subscriptions without their consent. Apple has not yet commented, but has taken two steps indicating that the company takes the accusations seriously … more…
fullText:
Repair technician turned consumer rights advocate Louis Rossmann recently accused Apple store staff of signing up customers to the company’s services subscriptions without their consent.

Apple has not yet commented, but has taken two steps indicating that the company takes the accusations seriously …

Rossmann is a repair technician who specializes in component-level logic board repairs and data recovery. He later became a key figure in advocating for right-to-repair legislation, which Apple initially opposed and later backed.

Apple store staff allegation

In a recent video, he claimed that some Apple store staff were signing up customers to trials of paid services subscriptions without their informed consent. Targets set by Apple are said to have encouraged the practice.

Customers accepting the offer of a personalized shopping experience could be shown the free trials of Apple services available to them based on their recent purchases. For example, buying an iPhone currently entitles you to a free three-month subscription to Apple TV. However, these trials automatically start debiting your payment method if you don’t cancel them before they end.

Staff were instructed to show these offers to customers and were allegedly set a 40% sign-up target, which Apple tracked as a performance metric. Crucially, the offers are shown on the employee’s device rather than on the customer’s phone. A store member told Rossman that some staff were hitting the Accept button without properly obtaining consent from customers in order to hit their target.

When I asked whether they’d seen a specialist press Agree with their own eyes, they answered “Yes, I saw some specialists press on behalf of the customer. So, they are hitting agree. They are signing the customer up to something without actually having the customer click okay, hit okay, or provide express consent.”

The store member also claimed that staff were describing the offer as a gift, which further disguised the fact that it would turn into a paid recurring subscription unless canceled.

Apple briefs staff and removes metric

	

At the time of writing, Apple has not responded directly to the accusations, but in a follow-up video yesterday Rossman cites a staff member describing the company’s response.

He says a memo was read out in the morning meeting stating that only customers could press the Accept button, and internal systems indicate Apple is no longer grading staff on the signup metric.

We have reached out to Apple for comment and will update with any response.

title: Report: iPad shipments drop 27.5% as global tablet market plunges in Q3
snippet: Despite global iPad shipments dropping 27.5% year-over-year in the third calendar quarter, Apple maintained its lead in the tablet market, according to a new report released today. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Despite global iPad shipments dropping 27.5% year-over-year in the third calendar quarter, Apple maintained its lead in the tablet market, according to a new report released today. Here are the details.

Apple still tops the market, despite steep shipment drop

According to a new report published by Omdia (via MacMagazine), Apple shipped 11,5 million iPads during Q3 2026, accounting for 36% of all shipments.

Compared to Q3 2025, that was a 27.5% drop in shipments, and a 2.2 percentage-point decline in market share.

For context, the global tablet market saw a 23% year-over-year drop, with total shipments going from 41.8 million to 32.2 million units. Omdia noted this was the lowest level in nearly three years.

As for Apple’s competitors, Samsung remained in second place with 16.9% market share, followed by Lenovo with 12.7%, Xiaomi with 7.3%, and Huawei with 5.7%.

	

When it comes to shipment growth, Lenovo was the only company among the top five to post a positive result, up 11.9% year over year. Huawei saw the steepest decline at 43%, followed by Apple at 27.5%, Samsung at 21.7%, and Xiaomi at 10.6%.

Commenting on the results, Omdia Research Manager Himani Mukka said supply constraints are “limiting vendors’ ability to deliver meaningful specification upgrades, leaving fewer compelling differences between new models and their predecessors.”

“As a result,” she added, “consumers are increasingly expected to delay purchases until more substantial improvements become available.”

title: Big Googlebook November update rolling out with 31 fixes, improvements
snippet: Just over a month after the launch, Google is rolling out the “Googlebook November update” with “many bug fixes, stability improvements, and firmware updates.” more…
fullText:
Just over a month after the launch, Google is rolling out the “Googlebook November update” with “many bug fixes, stability improvements, and firmware updates.”

There are updates across seven areas. Google first lists changes that benefit all users before detailing device-specific improvements. The HP (eight) and Dell XPS (nine) models see the most updates.

Security Updates: All Googlebook devices are updated with the latest security patches

Inputs & Desktop System UI

	

Keystrokes now register consistently when typing in a password or PIN on the lock screen immediately after waking the laptop from sleep or opening the lid

Removed the extra pop up notification when copying files inside of the Files app

Fixed an issue where Wallpaper & Style app hung or crashed in some cases when browsing wallpaper options

Settings > Tips & support now opens the official Googlebook Help Center

Settings > Devices & accessories > Physical keyboard now shows “Built in Keyboard” 

Improved built-in keyboard and touchpad responsiveness after folding laptop into tablet or tent mode and folding it back to laptop mode [Acer Googlebook 14] 

Improved touch responsiveness and reliability [Dell XPS Googlebook 13] 

Display, Graphics, & Video Conferencing

Improved stability for the Zoom app when using Background Blur, Virtual Backgrounds, Video Filters or 3D Avatars

External desktop wallpaper will no longer cover the built-in laptop display or hide the desktop taskbar and app icons when unplugging dual external monitors

Fixed an issue where playing DRM-protected video (such as Netflix) on a connected external monitor displayed a black video screen in some cases while audio continues playing [HP Googlebook 14] [Dell XPS Googlebook 13] 

Fixed an issue where pausing a protected video on an external monitor for more than 5 seconds caused the external monitor screen to go black in some cases [HP Googlebook 14] [Dell XPS Googlebook 13] 

Fixed a display driver crash that could cause the laptop to restart when unplugging a USB-C hub or DisplayPort daisy-chained (MST) multi-monitor setup. [HP Googlebook 14] [Dell XPS Googlebook 13] 

Fixed an issue where playing 60 FPS HDR/HLG videos in indoor lighting caused the screen backlight to dim unexpectedly in some cases while oversaturating on-screen UI colors and flickering [HP Googlebook 14] [Dell XPS Googlebook 13] 

	

Bluetooth, Audio

Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) mice now automatically reconnect after restarting the laptop

External USB microphones and USB audio interfaces (such as Focusrite Scarlett and Elgato Wave microphones) no longer face an audio buffering issue that prevents recording audio in some cases

Improved Bluetooth audio routing which fixes noticeable audio-to-video lip-sync lag when watching videos (such as YouTube) with Bluetooth headphones and earbuds [HP Googlebook 14] [Dell XPS Googlebook 13] 

Updated audio routing algorithm so connected Bluetooth Low Energy (ASHA) hearing aids could be selected for audio output (instead of playing through the built-in laptop speakers) [HP Googlebook 14] [Dell XPS Googlebook 13] 

System Performance

Improved browser memory stability when running heavy browser tab workloads

Stability improvements made to background systems supporting WiFi

Improved memory usage for on-device AI, improving multitasking stability on 16GB devices [Acer Googlebook 14] [ASUS Googlebook 14] [Lenovo Googlebook 15] 

Resolved a firmware installation issue that caused some devices to fall back to factory boot firmware and experience unexpected restarts during idle or normal use [HP Googlebook 14] [Dell XPS Googlebook 13] 

Stability fixes were made on the Linux 6.18 kernel [Acer Googlebook 14] [ASUS Googlebook 14] [Lenovo Googlebook 15] 

Updated the Linux 6.12 kernel with the latest Android 16 security patches, USB-C DisplayPort stability fixes, display suspend/resume watchdog crash fixes, and Multi-Stream DisplayPort HDCP 1.x content protection support [HP Googlebook 14] [Dell XPS Googlebook 13] 

Linux Terminal (BETA) 

Fixed several stability issues resulting in Improved reliability for interfaces between the terminal and Antigravity

Linux terminal shell sessions will maintain connection when laptop exits sleep mode user switches between tabs

Forward TCP ports (including SSH connections on port 2222) maintain connection during rapid port updates or after opening and closing multiple terminal processes

Fixed an issue where in some cases clicking an inactive tab accidentally closed it, preventing it from shutting down the Linux VM while other windows remain open 

System updates now refresh Linux VM configuration files in-place without resetting the user’s Linux storage or removing custom openssh-server configurations

Hardened system logging to ensure keystrokes and console output inside the Linux Terminal are never written to system diagnostic logs

Update Reliability

Fixed a boot-slot priority issue that could cause a device to enter a repeated reboot loop if an update was interrupted
